title: What is known about 1RB0LE_1RC---_1RD1RE_1LA0RF_0RC0LA_0LC0RB
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LE_1RC---_1RD1RE_1LA0RF_0RC0LA_0LC0RB.
intro: This six-state, two-symbol Turing machine was one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. It does not halt from blank tape: Lean proves it with the kernel alone, from a table of phase rules proved for all sizes and a linear invariant on the phase forms. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: It never halts. Lean proves nonhalting (kernel only; axioms propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound). From blank tape the machine reaches a phase form whose counts satisfy an invariant Good, a set of linear inequalities, and every move of the branch table (one cycle iterate and one exit rule, 20 cases) leads, after at least one step, to a form that satisfies it again.

What it does. The run alternates between two kinds of phase. In a right phase the head never visits the left end: the tape is (1110)a (1111110)k 111 001 (10)m, and each visit to the right end moves one copy from the run of 10 to the run of 1111110, keeping k + m fixed. In a round-trip phase the tape seen from the left end is 0… (1000)a (10)b wc with the 14-cell word w = 00000010000010 (two copies of the old 7-cell word rewritten); c falls while a and b grow, and when c reaches 0 the next right phase starts. Each phase is longer than the previous one (round-trip phases from 0.8 to 2.0·106 and from 6.4 to 20.8·106 steps), which is why the tape grows like the square root of time on average but in bursts.

Where a halt would come from. Only B reading a 1 halts. B is entered from A reading a 0 and from F reading a 1, both stepping right; so A>0 1 and F>1 1 halt (halt_A, halt_F). In the run B always reads a 0.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (B1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 56,767 cells have been visited and 20,806 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: sqrt/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.465). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.529).

claims.title: Every way to a halt
claims.text: Two steps before any halt the machine is in 0 D>x 1 1, D>1 1 1 or 0 D>0; no other configuration halts within three steps.

claims.title: Five passes
claims.text: C moving right crosses (10)n unchanged; A moving left crosses (01)n (8 steps a copy); F turns (1000)n into (1110)n and B turns 0 (0001)n into (1110)n 0 moving right; A turns (0111)n into (0010)n moving left. All for any n.

claims.title: The halting situations
claims.text: A>0 1 and F>1 1 halt after two steps; these are the only ways into B reading a 1.

claims.title: A right phase
claims.text: From step 1,896,095 to about 6.38·106 the head never reaches the left end. At the right-end visits the tape is (1110)170 (1111110)k 111 001 (10)m with k + m = 578 (k = 12 at step 2,148,568, 468 at step 6,188,728).

claims.title: A round-trip phase
claims.text: At the left-end visits from 824,136 to 1,896,095 the tape is 0… (1000)a (10)b wc plus short joints, with (a, b, c) going from (80, 219, 59) to (165, 555, 3). The next such phase starts at step 6,384,890 with c = 287.

claims.title: The 4-visit cycle, for all sizes
claims.text: Inside an odd round-trip phase the left-end visits repeat a cycle of four tape shapes. With S1 a b c = 0∞ A> 07 (1000)a 0000 1 00000 1 000 (10)b (00100000100000)c 001 00000 1 000 101, the machine goes from S1 a (b+2) (c+2) to S1 (a+3) (b+14) c in 80a + 72b + 1356 steps, for all a, b, c; cycle_iter applies it k times. Step 824,136 from blank is S1 80 219 59; the same cycle, with (a, b, c) = (30424, 87941, 19564), is running at step 1.044·1011 (c/phases.c).

claims.title: The two cycles of an even phase
claims.text: An even round-trip phase runs a 5-visit cycle on T3 a x d y z c = 07 (1000)a (10)x (0010)d (10)y 0000 1 00000 1 000 (10)z (00100000100000)c …, which goes to (a+4, x+8, d−5, y+7, z+5, c−2), and then a 3-visit cycle on T2 a x y c = 07 (1000)a 0000 1 00000 1 000 (10)x 0 (01)y (00000001000001)c 000 101, which goes to (a+3, x+7, y+5, c−2). Both are proved for all sizes, with their k-fold iterates.

claims.title: A whole odd phase and the right phase after it
claims.text: With O a b c = 0∞ A> 07 (1000)a (10)b (00001000001000)c 101 and EF a q = 0∞ E> 00000 (0001)a (00000100000001)q 00000 1 07 1 00000 1 000 101: from O a (2p+7) (2j+3) the machine reaches EF (a+4+3j) (p+6j+8), for all a, p, j. The proof chains the entry into the 4-visit cycle, j turns of it, the exit into a right phase, the right-phase cycle (one copy of 10 becomes one copy of 1111110, proved for any number of turns) and the start of the next even phase. The odd phases starting at steps 29,301, 808,896 and 27,629,379 (O 14 37 11, O 79 219 61, O 467 1283 361) meet its conditions, and the even phases the simulation finds next are EF 30 47, EF 170 288 and EF 1008 1720.

claims.title: The branch table, for all sizes
claims.text: Besides the cycles and odd_phase, Lean proves for all values of the parameters: the entry of an even phase, EF (a+7) (q+5) → T3 5 14 a 8 7 (q+2); the five exits of its 5-visit cycle by the number d < 5 of 0010 left (d = 0, 3, 4: two runs of 10 merge into T2; d = 1, 2: three runs, the middle one frozen, form U3); the 4-visit cycle of U3; the exits of the two- and three-run round trips into right phases RG and RG3, for both parities of the 14-cell words left; the cycles of those right phases; their ends when the run of 1111011 has even length (into O, or into T2); and the exit of the 4-visit cycle with no 14-cell word left (sexit0, into the right phase RF). lean/Ends.lean adds the other parities: RG and RG3 ending with an odd run of 1111011 start a 5-visit round trip T3 directly (gendo', g3endo'), and RF ending with an even run of 1111110 gives O a 0 c (rende'), which is an S1 after one pass (ozero, t3_s1). With these every form has a rule for each residue of its counts. Every rule is a symbolic run checked by the kernel, followed by a re-bracketing proof. Each rule states its exact step count.

claims.title: The table carries the run to step 5.7·10<sup>29</sup>
claims.text: From blank tape the machine reaches O 14 37 11 in 29,301 steps (blank_O). From there, 196 moves, each a rule of the table or a k-fold iterate of a cycle with concrete arguments, reach T2 34158019330534 128092572489511 160237983842729 41908435347077 (table_run, table_from_blank), at step 572,161,236,689,394,206,666,641,378,531 by the rules' step counts. The first odd right-phase end, RG 3564802 8141369 4104765 1 at step 1.08·1015, is among them. py/table.py 1e300 writes the 2,280 moves to step 5.6·10299, which Lean also checks (about 90 seconds).

claims.title: The replay agrees with the simulation up to 3·10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: py/macro.py replays the run with the table's rules only and predicts 49 configurations before step 3·1010, each with its exact step. The plain C simulator (c/checkpoints.c) finds every one of them on the tape at exactly that step: state, head position and every cell. The phase boundaries of c/boundaries.c (29,301, 191,775, 808,896, 6,370,604, 27,629,379, 223,234,215, 3,043,404,308, 22,249,365,380) are among them. So within 3·1010 steps every branch the run takes is in the table.

claims.title: The invariant
claims.text: Good gives, for each of ten forms (O a b c with b large, O a 0 c, S1, RF, EF, T3, T2, U3, RG, RG3), 3 to 16 linear inequalities with integer coefficients: the growing counts keep their ratios in a polyhedral cone that every move maps strictly inside the next one; the bounded counts stay in range and T3, U3, RG3 keep exact relations (for example x = 2a + 4 in T3); and a positive linear size, which every move multiplies by at least 1.1, stays above a threshold. These give every offset the rules need, and c ≥ 2⌊d/5⌋ + 3 in T3, so the 5-visit cycle never runs out of words. good_step proves each of the 20 cases with one move lemma and omega; the end of table_from_blank satisfies Good (decide).

claims.title: It does not halt from blank tape
claims.text: From good_step and table_from_blank: the run from blank tape is defined for every length. #print axioms nonhalting lists propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound; no native_decide.

claims.title: How the invariant was found
claims.text: Not part of the proof. The forms' counts at the form entries along the replay, divided by their sum, give a cloud of points per form. A fixpoint of linear programs over the 20 moves (homogeneous parts, margin 10-3) enlarges their convex hulls until each move maps every cone inside the next; a second linear program finds the size function. Along the replay every form entry from the 39th on satisfies Good.
claims.where: scratch scripts (scipy); the resulting inequalities are the data in py/closed.py

explainer.lede: It never halts, and Lean proves it. This machine alternates between long stays at its right end and rounds of full sweeps, each phase longer than the last; every way one phase can lead to the next is proved for all sizes, and linear inequalities on the counts show the run always stays where those rules apply. This page runs it in your browser.

facts.text: Proved in Lean by the kernel: a table of phase rules and a linear invariant on the counts.

sections.heading: The whole argument in one picture
html: This page walks through the Lean proof that this machine, started on a blank tape, never halts. You do not need to know Lean or Turing machine theory. Each step says what is claimed, shows it on the real machine in your browser, and says what checks it. Here every piece is checked by Kernel, Lean's small trusted core. The proof uses no native_decide and no compiled code.
The idea of the proof is an invariant: a description of a set of tapes, called good, with three properties.
• The run reaches a good tape. From the blank tape the machine reaches a good tape. It gets there after about 5.7·1029 steps, by 196 moves that are each a proved rule.
• A good tape always leads to another good tape. From any good tape the machine makes at least one step, without halting, and arrives at a good tape again.
• So the machine never halts. Repeating step 2 forever gives runs of every length. A machine that halts only has runs up to some fixed length.

A tape is "good" when it has one of ten shapes, called forms. Each form is a short pattern with some numbers in it, and those numbers must satisfy a list of linear inequalities, such as 534·b ≤ 1321·a + 321·c. The rest of this page explains the forms, the rules that take one form to the next, and why the inequalities keep holding.

sections.heading: How it could halt, and what the proof has to show
html: The table has one missing entry: B reading a 1. That is the only way to halt. Two transitions lead into B: A reading a 0 (writes 1, moves right) and F reading a 1 (writes 0, moves right). So the machine halts exactly when the head reads A> 0 1 or F> 1 1 (Lean: halt_A, halt_F).

The proof never looks for these patterns directly. It shows something stronger: from the blank tape, for every number n, the first n steps are all defined. That is the Lean statement ¬ HaltsFromBlank, where HaltsFromBlank means "some step reaches a configuration with no transition".
Press Step to see a halt play out on a made-up tape.

sections.heading: The tape is a list of numbers
html: Watch the machine for a while and its tape turns out to be made of long runs of a few short words: 1000, 10, a 14-cell word such as 00001000001000, and a few others, with short fixed pieces between them. So the tape can be written as a form: a pattern with the run lengths as numbers. For example

is the form O a b c: the head in state A at the left end, then seven 0s, a copies of 1000, b copies of 10, c copies of the 14-cell word, and 101. The proof uses ten forms. Seven are seen with the head at the left end, in state A or E (the "round-trip" forms, counting O a 0 c separately), and three with the head at the right end, in state E (the "right-phase" forms). Pick one to see its shape:

The first time the run is in one of these forms is at step 29,301, in the form O 14 37 11. Lean proves this by running the machine (blank_O). Kernel Try it: the button runs the machine in your browser and compares the tape with the form, cell for cell. In the picture below each cell is a thin bar (dark = 1), and the coloured band under it shows which run of the form it belongs to.
<canvas class="pw-bar" id="pw-startbar" width="900" height="60" aria-label="The tape at step 29,301, cell by cell"></canvas>

sections.heading: Crossing a run in one move
html: Between turns the head sweeps across the long runs. A run of a million copies would take millions of steps to simulate. But what happens to a run is simple, and Lean proves it once for every length:
• pass_10_right: C crosses (10)^n to the right in 2n steps and leaves it unchanged.
• pass_10_left: A crosses (01)^n to the left in 8n steps (it carries 10 along).
• fill_F: F turns (1000)^n into (1110)^n, 10 steps a copy.
• fill_B: B turns (0001)^n into (0111)^n, 10 steps a copy.
• clear_A: A, going left, turns (0111)^n into (0010)^n, 10 steps a copy.

Each is proved by running one copy for real (rfl: the kernel computes those few steps) and then a general lemma: if one copy takes the head through in the same state, n copies do too, in n times the steps. Kernel

sections.heading: One rule, for any size
html: Using these passes, Lean proves 27 rules. Each rule says: from form X with numbers like (a, b + 6, c + 2), the machine reaches form Y with numbers that are simple formulas of a, b, c, in an exact number of steps that is also a formula. The rule holds for every value of the variables. Kernel

The central example is the 4-visit cycle cycle: S1 a (b+2) (c+2) reaches S1 (a+3) (b+14) c in exactly 80a + 72b + 1356 steps. Each turn uses up two of the 14-cell words (c drops by 2), and the runs of 1000 and 10 grow by 3 and 12. The head visits the left end four times on the way.

Each rule's proof is a symbolic run: Lean steps the machine on a tape whose runs have lengths like b + 2, uses a pass to cross a whole run at once, and at the end shows the tape it got is the target form (by regrouping, e.g. (0010)^a 0 = 0 (0100)^a). Lean also proves the k-fold repeats such as cycle_iter, by induction on k.

Try any rule: choose small numbers for its variables, and the browser runs the real machine for exactly the stated number of steps. The picture shows the tape over time (rows are moments, time going down; dark = 1) and the path of the head (orange line). The check compares the result with the target form, cell for cell.

sections.heading: Ten forms and how they lead into each other
html: Put the rules together and every form leads to another form. The graph shows all of them. A loop on a form is a cycle rule, which runs as long as there are words left to use up. Each arrow out of a form is an exit, chosen by what is left over: how many 14-cell words remain (c = 0 or 1), how many 0010 remain in T3 (d = 0 to 4), or whether the run just built has even or odd length. The thicker an arrow, the more often the first 196 moves of the run use it. Click a form to see its rules.

● round-trip form (head at the left end)
● right-phase form (head at the right end)
×n: times the first 196 moves use it
Form :

Not every arrow is safe for every size. A rule needs its numbers to be large enough (for oentry, b ≥ 6 and c ≥ 2), and some combinations have no rule at all, for example T3 running out of 14-cell words while 5 or more 0010 are left. Those are the gaps the invariant of Step 6 closes.

sections.heading: Following the rules from the blank tape
html: Start from O 14 37 11 at step 29,301 and apply the rules, one after another, on the numbers alone. A cycle that runs k times is one move, with its steps added up by a formula. After 196 moves the run is at

at step 572,161,236,689,394,206,666,641,378,531 (about 5.7·1029). Lean checks this chain move by move: each line of table_run is one rule with its variables filled in, and the kernel checks the arithmetic. Kernel

The table lists the 197 states. You can test the first ones against the plain machine: the button runs it from blank tape and checks, at each predicted step, that the tape is exactly the predicted form, cell for cell.

Columns: the step at which the run is in that state, the form and its numbers, the rule that takes it to the next state (with how many turns, for a cycle), and whether the state is good (Step 6). The plain run was also compared with the first 49 states, up to 3·1010 steps, by a C program (c/checkpoints.c). That check is separate from Lean.

sections.heading: Why the rules never run out
html: The 196 moves cover a finite stretch of the run. To go on forever the proof needs one argument that works for all later moves. That is the invariant Good in lean/Closed.lean: for each form, a list of 3 to 16 linear inequalities on its numbers. They say three kinds of things:

shape
the growing numbers keep their ratios inside a fixed region. For O a b c, b stays between about 1.7 and 4.2 times a, and c between about 0.3 and 2.3 times a, in the shaded region of the picture below.

small parts
the bounded numbers stay in range (in RF, k is 4 or 5), and some numbers keep exact relations (in T3, x = 2a + 4).

size
one weighted sum is at least about 108, such as 71·b ≥ 50,000,000 for O.

The picture shows, for the forms O and S1, the region that the ratio inequalities allow (shaded), and the ratios of every O or S1 state of the replay (dots). The ratios move around from phase to phase but stay in the region. Filled dots are good states. Hollow dots are early states, which are still too small for the size condition.

Why do the inequalities keep holding? Seen from one phase to the next, the run is a map on the ten forms with 20 cases: one cycle run to the end, then one exit. The cases are split by the remainder of the count the cycle uses up (c mod 2, d mod 5) or the parity of the run just built. In each case the new numbers are fixed linear formulas of the old ones (lemmas mv_*). So the step from Good to Good is a question about linear inequalities, which Lean's omega procedure decides. Kernel Each case works because:
• the map sends each form's region strictly inside the next form's region, with room to spare;
• the size grows by a factor of at least 1.1 per case, so the room to spare grows faster than the fixed offsets in the formulas (the "+6", "+1356" and so on);
• the inequalities imply every condition a rule needs (b ≥ 6 and so on), and that T3 has enough 14-cell words for all its turns. That rules out the gaps of Step 4.

That is good_step: from a good tape the machine makes at least one step and reaches a good tape. The coefficients (up to 1,321) were found by linear programming on the replay's numbers, with scripts outside the proof. Lean does not trust them: if one were wrong, omega would fail.
The last state of the replay is good: Lean evaluates its 16 inequalities with decide (good_last). Kernel

sections.heading: What every piece rests on
html: Every piece of the proof, and what checks it. A wrong number anywhere, in the replay or the inequalities, cannot make the proof pass. It would only make one of the checks fail.

Rules.leanthe five passes, for any n; the two halting patternsKernel

#print axioms H113677.nonhalting lists only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, the three standard axioms of Lean's logic. There is no native_decide axiom: no compiled code is trusted anywhere in this proof.
The file lean/Blank.lean does contain one native_decide (a check that the first 107 steps do not halt), but nonhalting does not use it. It is a side fact, shown on the status page.

Other checks, separate from Lean Computed: the first 49 states of the replay match the plain run up to 3·1010 steps (c/checkpoints.c), and your browser can repeat the first ones in Step 5. The replay itself goes on without a gap to 10300 steps (2,281 states).

sections.heading: The last lines of the proof, in words
html: The end of lean/Closed.lean, theorem by theorem:

Good t
t is one of the ten forms, with numbers that satisfy that form's inequalities (gOp, gO0, gS1, gRF, gEF, gT3, gT2, gU3, gRG, gRG3).

good_step
from a good t, at least one step leads to a good t′. One case per form (step_Op … step_RG3), each split by remainder or parity into the 20 cases.

table_from_blank
some run from the blank tape ends at the last state of the replay (blank_O then table_run).

nonhalting
¬ HaltsFromBlank. By induction on N: for every N there is a run from blank of length at least N ending at a good tape. So runs of every length exist, and the machine does not halt.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.465). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.529).
After 109 steps the tape spans 56,767 cells (8,385 left of the start, 25,003 right), with a density of 1s of 0.367.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

family: phase machine: right-end accumulation alternating with two-sided round trips
summary: Alternates between long phases at the right end, which turn a run of 10 into a run of 1111110 or 1111011, and phases of round trips, which use that run up while runs of 1000 and 10 grow on the left. A table of phase rules is proved in Lean for all sizes, with a rule for every residue of the counts, and a linear invariant on the counts is restored by every rule; Lean proves it never halts (kernel only).
